courses.subject: JASP
courses.title: Japanese History: From Samurai to Salaryman
courses.description: This is an introductory course to Japanese history from ancient to contemporary times. Beginning with the peopling of the Japanese archipelago, the course offers a sweeping coverage of the major historical transformations that Japan has passed through from its ancient to modern times. The first half of the course will explore the people, institutions, and ideas and processes that form what we know of “traditional” Japan. The second half of the course will deal with the modern era, where Japan underwent one of the most striking transformations in world history. In the process, students will learn about different approaches to the study of Japan and will use Japan as a window through which we can better understand the dilemmas of modernity that challenge us all.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. Students will understand major transitions in Japanese history from ancient to medieval and modern times.
2. Students will learn how scholars and historians approach the study of Japanese history.
3. Students will learn history through reading a range of primary and secondary sources.
4. Students will be able to reflect on Japan to learn about transformations in global history.

courses.subject: JASP
courses.title: Modern Japanese Literature
courses.description: This course introduces representative works of Japanese literature—fiction, poetry, essay—from the modern era (1868–present), exploring cultural values represented in literary form by modern Japanese writers. The course is also an introduction to literary study, giving students the opportunity to develop the reading, writing, and speaking skills necessary to engage critically and imaginatively with literature in general. Taught in English. Texts vary with each offering of the course.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Students should be able to:

1. **Identify** representative works of Japanese literature and culture from the modern period (1868–present).
2. **Explore** cultural values represented by modern Japanese writers, which may include self and gender, aesthetics and beauty, religious faith, science and technology, humans and the natural world, as well as the art of literary expression.
3. **Build** critical and imaginative reading, thinking, and speaking skills through written assignments, class discussion, and presentation.
4. **Demonstrate** the literary significance of a modern Japanese work/writer through the successful completion of a final project or well-reasoned essay.

courses.title: Culture of Japanese Mass Media
courses.description: This course discusses the cultural and social implications of mass media in contemporary Japan. Media contexts in Japan are not only regarded as a business or an entertainment but also an ideology, or a remarkable source of soft power in the world's different media capitals. This course focuses on the construction of the Japanese mass media context in the age of internet and globalization, investigating how the media contexts are being produced and manipulated and how the influence is being demonstrated.

2. Students can analyze how the Japanese media influences our daily life

courses.title: Intimacy in Contemporary Japan
courses.description: How do people love, care, and desire in a changing world? Japan offers a rich terrain to explore this question, where shifting gender roles, evolving family forms, and diverse relational practices have long shaped public discussions about what counts as a “good” life and who gets to live it. Taking a feminist approach to intimacy as a world-making force that organizes life itself, this course examines how everyday relationships open onto the broader politics of living together. Throughout the semester, students will engage with feminist and queer theories to explore the themes of gender, sexuality, and family through various topics—from divorce and dating to hostess clubs, fandom love, self-marriage, pet families, and robotic companions. The course invites students to think about what worlds—of labor, affect, and belonging—intimacy makes possible, and how people inhabit them in Japan and beyond.
courses.learning_outcomes: By the end of this course, students will gain substantive knowledge of how gender, sexuality, and family shape the worlds of love, care, and desire in contemporary Japan. They will engage key social theories to analyze intimacy as a political force that organizes everyday life—its labor, affect, and belonging. Through close reading, discussion, and comparative reflection, students will develop critical skills to interpret cultural texts, connect ethnographic materials to theory, and articulate their own perspectives on the politics of living together in Japan and beyond.
courses.course_syllabus:
The course is organized into three thematic parts that move from the architecture of everyday life to the performance of desire and the politics of togetherness. Each week combines a lecture and a tutorial session: lectures provide historical and theoretical grounding, while tutorials invite close reading, discussion, and collaborative analysis of key texts and examples. Throughout the semester, students will engage with ethnographies, films, and theoretical writings to trace how intimacy works as a world-making force that shapes labor, emotion, and belonging in Japan. Two tutorial sessions will be reserved for review, group presentations, or other activities.

Part I. Home and Work: The Architecture of Gender/Sexuality in Everyday Life

Explores how the post-WWII ideals of family structured everyday life and how these arrangements are reconfigured in response to economic precarity and demographic change.

Themes: feminist political economy, care work, the family-state nexus.

Part II. Desire and Fantasy: The Performance and Discipline of Masculinity/Femininity

Examines gender/sexuality as performance and discipline through the worlds of hosts, hostesses, and media fantasies, linking emotion, sexuality, and labor.

Themes: performativity, affective labor, commodified sexuality.

Part III. Love and Kinship: The Politics and Ethics of Togetherness

Considers how new forms of love and kinship—fandom, pet families, solo marriage, and robotic companionship—redefine what it means to care for each other and live together.

Themes: intimate publics, (non)human companionship, relational ethics.

courses.title: Introduction to Japanese Economy
courses.description: This course introduces different aspects of the Japanese economy. Major topics include industrial structure, employment, trade, foreign investment and finance. Special emphasis will be put on the analysis of their structure, government policies and current problems.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Learning outcome: After completing this course, students should be able to:

- state, recognize, recall and tell the main features of the Japanese economy

- describe and clarify the strengths and weaknesses, the advantages and disadvantages of these features

- compare and contrast Japanese economic developmental phases

- apply, relate and deepen their appreciation of the significance of the dynamics and interaction of Japanese domestic economy, external political economic/trade relations and the recent trend of production networking/regionalism/integration.

- analyze Japan's structure, government policies, economic relations and current trends.

- generalize, reflect and hypothesize their own conclusions with regards to the course materials and contemporary issues

[Writing skills]

Through the graded short essay exercise required in the course, class participants develop skills in essay-writing and library research such as literature review and analytical skills. It is also an opportunity for participants to put their creative ideas in writing.

[Interactive skills]

Class participation and attendance facilitates interactions with other class participants, learning from each other and exploring alternative viewpoints. The graded tutorials enhance interactions with other class participants, learning from each other and exploring alternative viewpoints through oral presentations that include class discussions and debates. Subject to availability, guest lectures may also be possible as opportunities for class participants to interact with individuals with specific relevant expertise.

[Test-taking skills]

Class participants are required to take the mid-term quiz to gauge their ability to keep up with materials midway through the course, test-taking skills and an opportunity for class participants to test their own knowledge. The final exam evaluates class participants¡¦ overall understanding of the course materials and performance in the second half of the course.

[Reading skills]

While lectures and tutorials are the main modes of knowledge exchange and learning activity, students are encouraged to critically examine the required readings and present their alternative viewpoints and comments in the tutorials.
courses.course_syllabus:
Course Description

Japan's postwar economic development has become a model by itself, characterized by state-led development, unique Japanese economic features, fast-growth and is also in the midst of reforms and demographic adaptation to cope with new challenges. To understand contemporary Japanese economy, it may be just as important to study its developmental phases. After the fast-growth period, while observers are keen to see how Japan will cope domestically with its long recession. Both internal and external economic dynamics interact to form the basis of Japan's economy. No prior knowledge of economics is needed beyond the usual understanding of terms that one typically finds in the mass media (ie layman understanding). It utilizes some the materials of some of the most influential economists in Japan including Nakamura Takafusa (University of Tokyo) and cutting-edge works by Western scholars. The course is a survey that does not pretend to be exhaustively but nevertheless gives its participants a firm foundation in understanding Japanese economic development. The course can be broadly divided into three main sections of historical development, contemporary developments and case studies.

courses.title: Asia at War
courses.description: World War II remains the most total and bloodiest conflict in world history. Fought on multiple fronts on three continents, the war witnessed a complex mesh of ideologies and war aims. It wrought unparalleled destruction and targeted civilians to an unprecedented degree. It has been the only war to date in which atomic weapons were used. The war pitted empires against each other and led to the fall of many of those global empires. This course will focus on World War II in Asia. It uses Japanese history as a window into global processes, and also places the war in its proper regional context. Beginning with World War I, this course journeys through the crisis of East Asian international relations in 1920s and 1930s to the outbreak of a multi-front war in East and Southeast Asia. It considers the war’s impact on empires and nations, soldiers and victims, and peoples throughout the region. And it explores the legacies that remain visible across the region today.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. Understand the causes and legacies of World War II in Asia. In the process, they will learn the ways in which the war helped shape the contemporary world.
2. Read academic works and learn to clearly articulate the main arguments of academic writing.
3. Engage confidently in class-time debates and improve their argumentative reasoning.
4. Write research papers that make use of primary source documents (the documents analyzed can be in any language).
5. Understand historical events from multiple perspectives, and become more critical of primary source documents.
courses.course_syllabus:
Week 1: Introduction and Course Outline

Week 2: World War I and Empires at War

This week focuses on World War I in Asia, the emergence of Japan as a world power during the wartime years, and Japanese wartime imperialism in China and the Asia-Pacific.

Week 3: Aftermath of War: The Washington System and its Discontents

This week centers on the dramatic global postwar rejection of the diplomacy of imperialism and war that was symbolized by the "Washington System". It was this system that Japan would seek to change and then overthrow in the 1930s.

Week 4: The Global Depression and Crisis in Manchuria

This week focuses on the issues leading to the Manchurian Incident of September 1931 and the renewed Japanese imperialism of the 1930s.

Week 5: Ultranationalism, Insubordination, Rebellion, and the Question of Fascism

Japan's renewed imperialism was accompanied by ultranationalism in society and insubordination and even rebellion with the military. This class will use these issues to question the nature of Japanese "facism".

Week 6: Japan and China: Toward Total War

This week focuses on the lead up to and the initial stages of Japan's total war in China from 1937.

Week 7: Japan Lashes Out! The Attacks of December 8, 1941

This week will focus on the beginning of the Pacific War, or the so-called War for Greater East Asia. Students will have a fun group activity for the majority of the class to try to avoid the war from happening!

Week 8: Asia Under Japan

This week will show how Japan sought to rule much of Asia, and how its efforts changed throughout the course of the war.

Week 9: The War in Everyday Life

This week will show the impact the war had on daily life in Japan.

Week 10: Learning How to Die

This week will focus on the cultural history of fighting a losing war, and how that led Japanese government and mass media to enshrine death as a meaningful way to fight.

Week 11: Endgame: The Japanese Surrender

This week will center on the events surrounding the Japanese surrender, including the controversial decisions to use firebombing and atomic weaponry as weapons of war.

Week 12: From War to Peace

This week will focus on how the war's end reshaped Japan, its empire and the region.

Week 13: The War in Retrospect: Legacies and Memories

This final week will continue to show the extraordinary legacies of the age of total war on both Japan and Asia.

courses.description: This course equips students with foundational skills for translating English into Japanese and introduces the basic knowledge necessary for improving quality. Texts are drawn from current events in newspapers, magazines, social media, academic journals and books. Advisory: Not for students who have studied for one year or more in Japan.

courses.learning_outcomes:
1. Understand the strength and weakness of a variety of translation methods.
2. Recognize text types and their conventions, formulate best approaches for translating different types of texts, and reflect on strategies for problem solving.
3. Develop the ability to reflect on the process of translation.
4. Apply linguistic and sociocultural knowledge to produce translations from English to Japanese.

courses.feedback_evaluation:
* Translation practice: Students will be assigned one piece of text (250 words) to practice their translation skills.
* Translation project: Each student will produce a translation of a set text of 800 words accompanied by a 400-word reflective commentary outlining the student’s self-reflections on the strategies and procedures that s/he has employed for this translation project. The commentary may also address such questions as: How is your experience of doing this project related to what you have learned about translation during this course? In what way(s) has this project been beneficial for you? How might it be beneficial in the future, both for you and for others?
* Presentation: Students will work in groups of 3-4 members on a translation exercise relating to a topic of their choosing. Each group will translate an English text of 1500 words into Japanese and present to the whole class a summary of the work they have undertaken in the process of planning the project, researching the topic and translating the text.
* In general, the summary should introduce the text (What is the text you chose to translate? Why did you choose this text? What do you particularly like about this text? What does your reader need to know about the author of the text? What does your reader need to know about the context from which the source text emerged?, etc.), and address the group’s choice of translation approach(es) and difficulties encountered in the exercise in both general terms and specific to English – Japanese translation (What are the conventions of the chosen text type? What similar texts did you use as your reference? What difficulties did you anticipate in the translation? What theoretical approach to translation did you follow? What translation strategies and techniques did you adopt and why? Did you encounter cultural problems in your translation? What process did you follow in preparing the translation? How did you solve the anticipated problems? Are you satisfied with your solutions? Where are you dissatisfied? Who or what sources helped you? How did you organize your work as a group?, etc.).
* Active participation: Assessed on each student’s engagement in class discussions, groupwork and practical translation tasks in-class.

courses.description: This course examines Japanese culture through anthropological perspectives. The course will consider how people in Japan experience family life, work and intimate relationships. It also covers cultural ideals such as the self, gender roles and aesthetic forms. The lectures will explain how anthropological perspectives have been used to study Japan. The course encourages students to consider how anthropological methods and approaches can be used to study Japan as well as their own societies.

courses.learning_outcomes:

Students will learn discourse patterns, vocabulary and expressions which are essential in writing memos, e-mails, commercial product descriptions, and oral presentation handouts. courses.description: This course explores methods and approaches used by anthropologists in studying Japan. The course provides students with an anthropological framework for research on Japan. The course will also introduce theoretical approaches and concepts used by anthropologists studying Japan. 2) use anthropological approaches to discuss basic trends in the social development of modern Japan.

The course also examines current gender relations and roles in a variety of arenas of life such as families, corporations, communities, political groups, schools, and in the mass media.

courses.subject: JASP
courses.title: Advanced English-Japanese Translation
courses.description:
This course introduces some of the key concepts in translation theory and focuses on their application to English to Japanese translation practice. The course provides students who have a solid knowledge of basic Japanese with a practical experience of translation and aims to develop their translation skills to a high level of proficiency.

Students will work with a wide range of text types, become familiar with different translation techniques, and develop intellectual perspectives on the activity of translation.

Texts are drawn from various sources including news media, internet, business communication, academic literature, fiction and films. Students are required to pass a placement test or obtain equivalent competence in Japanese before course registration.

For students of MPhil-PhD Japanese Studies & MA Japanese Studies
Exclusion= JASP4380
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. Apply linguistic and sociocultural knowledge to produce translations from English to Japanese.
2. Recognize text types and their conventions, formulate best approaches for translating different types of texts, and reflect on strategies for problem solving.
3. Develop the ability to reflect on the process of translation.
4. Learn to analyze the relationship between translation and culture.
courses.course_syllabus:
Week 1: Introduction to translation studies

Week 2: Skills and knowledge necessary to work as a successful translator

Week 3: Translation strategies, methods, approaches, and different degrees of freedom (literal, free, semantic, communicative,

or adaptation)

Week 4: Techniques for translating different text types (literary, academic, business, and media)

Week 5: Techniques commonly adopted in English – Japanese translation (omission, expansion, and changing parts of text)

Week 6: Difficulties specific to English – Japanese translation (rhetorical devices, proverbs, and idioms)

Week 7: Methods for translating culture-specific items (transcription, naturalization, localization, and cultural equivalent)

Week 8: Translation and culture, interlingual translation and intralingual translation

Week 9: Computer-aided human translation and machine translation

Week 10: Oral dimension, consecutive interpreting and simultaneous interpreting

Week 11: Group presentation

Week 12: Group presentation

Week 13: Review and conclusions
courses.feedback_evaluation:
Assignment: Students will be assigned one piece of homework (500 words) to practice their translation skills.

• Translation project: Each student will produce a translation of a set text of 1000 words accompanied by a 400-word reflective commentary outlining the student's selfreflections on the strategies and procedures that s/he has employed for this translation project. The commentary may also address such questions as: How is your experience of doing this project related to what you have learned about translation during this course? In what way(s) has this project been beneficial for you? How might it be beneficial in the future, both for you and for others?

• Presentation: Students will work in groups of 3-4 members on a translation exercise relating to a topic of their choosing. Each group will translate an English text of 2000words into Japanese and present to the whole class a summary of the work they have undertaken in the process of planning the project, researching the topic and translating the text.

In general, the summary should introduce the text (What is the text you chose to translate? Why did you choose this text? What do you particularly like about this text? What does your reader need to know about the author of the text? What does your reader need to know about the context from which the source text emerged?, etc.), and address the group's choice of translation approach(es) and difficulties encountered in the exercise in both general terms and specific to English – Japanese translation (What are the conventions of the chosen text type? What similar texts did you use as your reference? What difficulties did you anticipate in the translation? What theoretical approach to translation did you follow? What translation strategies and techniques did you adopt and why? Did you encounter cultural problems in your translation? What process did you follow in preparing the translation? How did you solve the anticipated problems? Are you satisfied with your solutions? Where are you dissatisfied? Who or what sources helped you? How did you organize your work as a group?, etc.).

• Active participation: Assessed on each student's engagement in class discussions,

groupwork and practical translation tasks in-class.

courses.subject: JASP
courses.title: Japanese Dialectology
courses.description: Although Japanese language learners usually take the “standard language” of Japanese as the learning target, there are many dialects in Japan and they can represent the cultural characteristics in that particular area. This course introduces the structure of dialect by comparing the differences between the “standard language” and one representative example of Japanese dialects: Kansai dialect. Students will learn how dialects reflect the culture and society in Japan through the perspectives of sociolinguistics. This course will use multi-media resources such as TV variety programs, dramas and comedy shows as teaching materials to illustrate the daily usage of dialects.

courses.learning_outcomes:

2. Students are expected to be able to identify various types of dialects by comparing the differences between dialect and standard language.

3. Students are expected to be able to use the approach of sociolinguistic analysis and find out how culture and society influence language usage.

courses.description:
This course introduces students to the main themes of Japanese literature from the ancient to the modern period. The texts covered include poetry, diaries, drama, and fiction. The social and cultural context in which the work was produced will be discussed. Each work will be discussed within larger trends in Japanese literature.

courses.title: Anthropology of Japan
courses.description: This course examines Japanese culture through anthropological perspectives. The course will consider how people in Japan experience family life, work and intimate relationships. It also covers cultural ideals such as the self, gender roles and aesthetic forms. The lectures will explain how anthropological perspectives have been used to study Japan. The course encourages students to consider how anthropological methods and approaches can be used to study Japan as well as their own societies.

In this semester it will introduce Japanese philosophy, which is an important topic for understanding the root of Japanese culture. Three areas will be discussed: 1) traditional Japanese thought such as Buddhism, Confucianism and Shinto/Native Studies thoughts; 2) modern Japanese philosophers such as Nishida Kitaro, Kuki Shuzo and Watsuji Tetsuro; and 3) topics related to Japanese philosophical thoughts.

courses.learning_outcomes: Upon completion of the course, students are expected to understand basic concepts of Japanese philosophy, and their influence on traditional and modern Japanese culture. They can critically read texts written by Japanese philosophers, and analyse Japanese cultural phenomena from a philosophical perspective.

courses.title: The Global Japanese
courses.description: This course examines Japanese migrants and communities in diverse locations such as East Asia, Oceania, Europe, and Americas. Through tracing historical experiences of Japanese emigrants (Nikkeijin) and exploring their transnational cultural practices, students will develop a picture of Japan’s changing roles in a globalized world from an aggressive colonizer to an economic superpower to a shrinking society. Topics may include the variegated roles of Japanese migrants in settler communities and colonial societies, gendered communities of practice, transnational networks and communication, linguistic and culinary hybridity, and Japanese migrants’ contribution to the global spread and dissemination of Japanese popular culture

courses.subject: JASP
courses.title: Anthropology of Japanese Popular Culture
courses.description:
This course offers an advanced seminar on Japanese popular and mass culture from anthropological perspectives. Thus this is not a survey course of different kinds of popular culture in Japan, but rather this course requires us to theoretically engage in social theories of popular/mass culture and analyze interpretations of meanings and forms of particular "popularly massified" socio-cultural phenomena in Japan.

The course first provides literature on the major classical and critical theories of the "culture industry" in Europe as well as the formation of mass society in Japan. Next, we will analyze the forms and meanings of the diverse, popularly massified culture of production and consumption by examining anthropological works on Japan. Specifically, this course examines the issues of popular culture and mass culture through four different spheres: culture industries, media consumption, material culture and fandom, and globalization. Through analyzing these four spheres, the course also traces the thematic issues of gender, class, and cultural politics in the context of modernization and globalization.

These issues provide the underlying structure and symbols that demonstrate how anthropologists approach a particular representation of complex popularized cultural movements under late capitalism.

courses.subject: JASP
courses.title: Asia and Asianism in Modern Japanese History
courses.description:
“Asia” is one of the core concepts of Japanese cosmopolitanism. In the modern era (19th-20th century), when the world dynamics were changing drastically, Japanese intellectuals tried to break away from the old East Asian order centered on China and put forward a new worldview to build up a modern Japanese national consciousness and regional order. The discussion of “Asia” is one of the specific attempts. This is an exploratory course that analyzes various Asian discourses from the perspectives of the history of Sino-Japanese relations, the history of East Asia, and the history of the world and discusses the process of change in Japan's understanding of Asia and the world from different perspectives, including history, ideology, politics, economics, literature, and culture.
The lectures cover the Asian (East Asian) understanding of China and Japan in ancient times, the Asian view and worldview of Japan in modern times, the interaction between the late Shogunate thinkers and the times, the activities and evolution of different Asianist organizations in the Meiji period, such as the Shinyasha (振亞社), the Koya-kai (興亞會), the Asia Society (亞細亞協會), the Toho-Kyokai (東邦協會), the Genyōsha (玄洋社), and the Kokuryū-kai (黑龍會), as well as the Asian views and interactions between the important thinkers of China and Japan such as Sun Yat-sen, Li Dazhao, Fukuzawa Yukichi, Okakura Tenshin, and others. It also explores the views of post-war Japan, China, Korea, the United States, India, and other countries on the Asian/East Asian conflicts and alliances, discussing the possibilities and challenges of the integration of post-war Asia or East Asia.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in Articulated M.Phil-Ph.D in Japanese Studies or MA in Japanese Studies
courses.learning_outcomes:
Students are expected to achieve the following goals after taking this course:

1. Using “views towards Asia” or “Asianism” as keywords, to understand the development of Japanese history and the dynamic changes in Japanese intellectuals' views on Asia and the world in the process of development; and to understand the inner dynamics of the changes in Japan's relationship with Asian countries and Asia as a whole.
2. To gain a new understanding of the various groups in modern Japan, especially the complex ideas of “Asianists”, including political leaders, intellectuals, samurai ronin, students, etc., and to recognize the contradictions and tensions within modern Japanese Asianist thought.
3. To express views on the development and change of modern Japanese thoughts clearly in Chinese, both in essay writing and oral presentation.

courses.subject: JASP
courses.title: Modern Japanese Literature
courses.description: This course introduces representative works of Japanese literature—fiction, poetry, essay—from the modern era (1868–present), exploring cultural values represented in literary form by modern Japanese writers. The course is also an introduction to literary study, giving students the opportunity to develop the reading, writing, and speaking skills necessary to engage critically and imaginatively with literature in general. Taught in English. Texts vary with each offering of the course.
courses.enrollment_requirement:
For students in Articulated M.Phil-Ph.D in Japanese Studies or MA in Japanese Studies.
Students who took JASP2020 are NOT allowed to take JASP5628.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Students should be able to:

1. **Identify** representative works of Japanese literature and culture from the modern period (1868–present).

2. **Explore** cultural values represented by modern Japanese writers, which may include self and gender, aesthetics and beauty, religious faith, science and technology, humans and the natural world, as well as the art of literary expression.

3. **Improve** critical and imaginative reading, thinking, and speaking skills through written assignments, class discussion, and presentation.

4. **Develop** the writing skills required for a graduate-level academic essay. Such skills include formulating a thesis, supporting an argument, organizing ideas clearly and logically, engaging with secondary sources, compiling a bibliography, and drawing conclusions in an effective way.
courses.course_syllabus:
* *Week 1**
Topic: Introduction to “Modern Japanese Literature”
- What is Modern Japanese Literature? What is close reading?

* *Week 2**
Topic: When East Meets West
Reading: Mori Ōgai, “The Dancing Girl” (1890)

* *Weeks 3–5**
Topic: The Modern Novel
Reading: Natsume Sōseki, Kokoro (1914)

* *Week 6**
Topic: Modern Lyricism
Reading: Selected poems by Yosano Akiko (1878–1942)

* *Week 7**
No class. Graduate students will conduct research at the library,

* *Week 8**
Topic: Japanese Aesthetics
Reading: Tanizaki Jun’ichirō, “In Praise of Shadows” (1933)

* *Week 9**
Topic: Film, Beauty, and Landscape
Reading: Selections from Kawabata Yasunari, Snow Country (1948)

* *Week 10**
Topic: Postwar Survival
Reading: Dazai Osamu, “Villon’s Wife” (1947)

* *Week 11**
Topic: Science and Seduction
Reading: Selections from Abe Kōbō, The Woman in the Dunes (1962)

* *Week 12**
Topic: Death and Renewal
Reading: Mishima Yukio, “Death in Midsummer” (1953)

* *Week 13**
Topic: Course Summary and Conclusion

courses.subject: JASP
courses.title: Japan-China Intellectual and Cultural Exchange in the Early Modern Period
courses.description: This course is designed to examine the introduction and localization of Chinese culture in Tokugawa Japan (1603-1868) through reading of primary sources and important academic writings in English, Japanese and Chinese. Issues such as the redefinition and appropriation of Confucian concepts, the interaction between Chinese learning and nativist learning, Chinese legends in Tokugawa Japan and the uses of Chinese terminology in Tokugawa historiography will be investigated through close reading of Tokugawa texts and small-group discussion.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in the Articulated M.Phil-Ph.D Programme in Japanese Studies
courses.learning_outcomes:
(1) study important works on Tokugawa intellectual history and Sino-Japanese relations.

(2) acquire basic skills in reading classical Chinese and Japanese in the Tokugawa style.

(3) prepare for Ph.D research.
courses.course_syllabus:
Part One (week 1-4): Basic readings on Tokugawa Intellectual History

Part Two: (week 5-8): Basic readings on Sino-Japanese relations in the early modern period.

Part Three (week 9-12): Readings of Tokugawa texts.

courses.subject: JASP
courses.title: Japanese Culture and Society in Regional and Global Perspectives
courses.description: This course examines the theoretical and conceptual approaches in studying Japanese society and culture from regional and global perspectives. The course considers changes in Japanese society and culture domestically as well as in relation to regional and global contexts. It explores the commonalities and differences in the experiences of globalization, demographic changes brought about by economic development, changes to the political system and civil society, as well as consumption and lifestyles in Japan and other Asia-Pacific regions and areas, including but not restricted to the US, China, Hong Kong. It also investigates how theoretical and methodological approaches have changed over time in examining Japanese society and culture due to increasing contributions made by scholars in comparative studies.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in the Articulated M.Phil-Ph.D Programme in Japanese Studies
courses.learning_outcomes:
At the completion of the course, students will be able to:

- identify and critique theoretical and conceptual approaches to Japanese society and its interactions with other societies.

- apply different methodological approaches to studying Japan and its interactions with other societies and cultures.

- critically analyze comparative approaches in the study of Japan.
